documents.unit: Rutgers Office of Information Technology (all campuses)
documents.title: Guidance on the use of AI at Rutgers
documents.summary: Universitywide Rutgers IT guidance for all campuses. It says AI rules vary by course and instructor, but AI is not permissible for coursework unless instructors say so. It also covers approved tools, confidential data, verifying output, and purchasing.
documents.stance_why: The page leaves details to instructors ('will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor'), but sets a default for coursework: AI tools 'should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors'. That is a ban unless permitted, so restrict rather than delegates.

units.why: The page says OIT 'provides access to generative AI tools with protections', which is a statement that the university supplies licensed tools; this fits P17 (sanctioned tool) and informs rather than binds.
units.anchor: provides access to generative AI tools with protections for use in university work.

units.why: Says 'your data will not be used to train the models' when using Rutgers-approved versions; this is a privacy fact about vetted tools, so P50 (protect data, prefer vetted tools) as informs.
units.anchor: your data will not be used to train the models underlying the tools

units.why: 'only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used at the university' is a directive to prefer vetted tools to protect data, matching P50; it is stated as should for all users, not only students.
units.anchor: only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used at the university

units.why: 'guidance ... will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor' leaves the rule to instructors, which is P04 (each instructor or course sets the rule).
units.anchor: AI tools in academic settings will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor
units.policy: Guidance on appropriate AI use in academic settings typically varies by discipline, course and/or instructor.

units.why: 'Faculty should consider providing guidance to students on the use of AI' asks instructors to communicate expectations; nearest is P09, but it does not say syllabus or assignment instructions.
units.anchor: consider providing guidance to students on the use of AI to support learning and coursework
units.fit_note: Asks faculty to consider giving students guidance on AI; it does not require a syllabus statement and is only a soft 'should consider'.

units.why: 'students are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors' tells students to check expectations with instructors, which is P10 (ask before using AI).
units.anchor: students are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors to understand any

units.why: 'should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors' sets the default when instructors are silent, which is exactly P06 (fallback rule) and restricts AI.
units.anchor: they should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors

units.why: 'Students are responsible for understanding and abiding by their program and instructors' guidance' makes students answerable for knowing the AI rules; this is not about owning submitted work (P29) and fits no other type well.
units.anchor: and abiding by their program and instructors’ guidance or rules on the use of AI
units.uncovered_note: Students are responsible for learning and following the program's and instructor's AI rules.

units.why: Quotes the integrity principle that coursework be 'the student's own and created without the aid of impermissible technologies'; this is the ownership rule P29, applied to AI by reference.
units.anchor: the student’s own and created without the aid of impermissible technologies, materials, or collaborations
units.fit_note: Ties ownership of coursework to the ban on 'impermissible technologies', which implicitly includes AI.

units.why: 'may not be appropriate for use in AI applications' warns against putting confidential data, PHI and proprietary information into AI; this is data protection, P50.
units.anchor: (PHI), and other proprietary Rutgers information may not be appropriate for use in AI applications

units.why: 'Always review and verify AI content and outputs' tells users to check AI output, which is P31; must because of 'Always'.
units.anchor: Always review and verify AI content and outputs.

units.why: 'You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content' puts responsibility for AI-assisted university work on the user, which is P29.
units.anchor: You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content

units.why: States AI tools 'may include copyrighted information without attribution', a copyright caution; P52 covers copyright of AI output, while the bias and inaccuracy clause is a fact about errors.
units.anchor: AI tools can produce biased and inaccurate information, and may include copyrighted information without attribution.
units.fit_note: Also says AI output can be biased and inaccurate, which is a verification caution (P31).

units.why: Purchases of AI applications 'must follow the same security processes and risk assessments' plus accessibility standards; an institutional vetting rule for AI vendors, P65.
units.anchor: you must follow the same security processes and risk assessments as for other software purchases
units.fit_note: Covers purchasing and accessibility review of AI applications, not vendor contracts or data sharing specifically.

units.why: Lists the Academic Integrity, Information Classification and Acceptable Use policies as 'particularly relevant for the use of AI'; AI use falls under existing policies, P77.
units.anchor: within the University Policy Library are particularly relevant for the use of AI at Rutgers.

documents.unit: OTEAR (Office of Teaching Evaluation and Assessment Research)
documents.title: AI in Education - OTEAR Rutgers
tiers: Sample 1: not permitted in any stage of writing
Sample 2: only to brainstorm and see examples; all submitted material your own
Sample 3: fully permitted with citation of the tool and ability to explain the work
documents.summary: An archived OTEAR page of advice to Rutgers faculty on AI: learn the tools, redesign assignments, write a clear course policy, and choose among sample syllabus statements. Much of the page is event listings and reading lists, which are not coded.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule itself; it tells instructors to 'Develop clear policies for each course' and offers three sample statements from ban to 'fully permitted', depending on 'whether AI tools will be banned or permitted'. That is delegation with tiers.

units.why: The unit says OTEAR runs 'workshops, discussions, and numerous resources' for faculty and staff on AI; faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: providing engaging workshops, discussions, and numerous resources

units.why: Says chatbot data was scraped 'usually without consent' and outputs may be 'biased'; names harms, P53.
units.anchor: scraped” from the Internet (usually without consent)
units.fit_note: Mixes data-consent and bias concerns with accuracy warnings.

units.why: Describes 'shared learning that we think of in terms of critical AI literacy' for students, staff and faculty; AI literacy framing, closest to P70 though no training is mandated.
units.anchor: a process of shared learning that we think of in terms of critical AI literacy
units.fit_note: Frames critical AI literacy as shared learning; it offers no training or module itself.

units.why: The AI Roundtable Council's document gives 'advice on academic integrity, a sample of statements for your syllabi' to faculty, i.e. support materials for instructors, P63.
units.anchor: a sample of statements for your syllabi, and a list of resources

units.why: 'Learn what AI tools can and cannot do ... before incorporating an AI tool into a class activity or restricting its use' advises instructors to learn the tools before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: Learn what AI tools can and cannot do

units.why: 'Test your assignments by submitting them to ChatGPT' is advice that instructors try their assignments in AI before setting policy; P63 covers faculty learning about AI.
units.anchor: Test your assignments by submitting them to ChatGPT and/or other AI tools

units.why: Tells faculty to 'become familiar with the student conduct requirements for charging students' if they restrict AI; relates to integrity processes (P36) but the content is faculty preparation.
units.anchor: Become familiar with the student conduct requirements for charging students with violations of academic integrity
units.fit_note: Advises instructors who restrict AI to learn the conduct procedures; it does not itself classify AI misuse as misconduct.

units.why: Suggests assignments 'that require students to use higher-order thinking ... are more difficult for students to answer using AI tools'; redesigning assignments around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Consider developing assignments that require students to use higher-order thinking

units.why: 'project-based learning or staged assignments that begin with work in class' restructures coursework in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: Also consider project-based learning or staged assignments that begin with work in class

units.why: 'Develop rubrics that emphasize critical thinking' changes the grading scheme in response to AI, which is P35.
units.anchor: Develop rubrics that emphasize critical thinking, application of knowledge, and evaluation of knowledge

units.why: 'Develop clear policies for each course' asks every instructor to state a course AI policy, which is P09; the sentence is a recommendation, so should.
units.anchor: Develop clear policies for each course.

units.why: Says to 'repeat the learning goals of the course and how these goals are important in the decision making process to ban or permit AI tools'; explaining rule reasons to students, P66.
units.anchor: repeat the learning goals of the course and how these goals are important

units.why: 'Depending on whether AI tools will be banned or permitted, add text that clearly states the conditions specific for the course' leaves the ban/permit decision to each course, P04.
units.anchor: Depending on whether AI tools will be banned or permitted, add text

units.why: Sample syllabus text 'not permitted in any stages of the writing process on any assignment' is a ban model, P01 (prohibit by default); it is offered as an option, not a university rule.
units.anchor: is not permitted in any stages of the writing process on any assignment.
units.fit_note: A sample statement instructors may adopt, not a mandated rule; writing-process wording is prose-oriented.

units.why: Sample text 'only permitted to help you brainstorm ideas and see examples' limits AI to brainstorming; P15 (brainstorming) best matches, with 'All material you submit must be your own' as the limit.
units.anchor: is only permitted to help you brainstorm ideas and see examples.
units.fit_note: Sample statement; the only allowed use is brainstorming and seeing examples.

units.why: Sample text 'All material you submit must be your own' states ownership of submissions (P29), separate from the brainstorming permission above.
units.anchor: All material you submit must be your own.

units.why: Sample text 'fully permitted, but you must cite the tool' makes AI allowed with citation, so default-permit P02; the citation and explanation duties are coded separately.
units.anchor: Use of AI such as ChatGPT is fully permitted
units.fit_note: A sample statement instructors may adopt; permission is conditional on citation and explanation.

units.why: 'you must cite the tool' requires disclosure of AI use with the submission, P24.
units.anchor: you must cite the tool

units.why: 'be able to explain any work that you submit' requires understanding of submitted work, P30.
units.anchor: be able to explain any work that you submit

units.why: 'Schools and departments should discuss these issues as the tools and their use evolve' recognizes that policy must be revisited, P54.
units.anchor: Schools and departments should discuss these issues as the tools and their use evolve.

units.why: 'OTEAR is available for consultation and discussion at any time' offers consultation to faculty, P63.
units.anchor: OTEAR is available for consultation and discussion at any time

units.why: FAQ defines ChatGPT and similar LLMs as 'software applications designed to respond in text to text-based questions'; a definition of the tools covered, P61.
units.anchor: software applications designed to respond in text to text-based questions

units.why: Says AI tools asked for sources 'frequently fabricate information and invent references'; a caution that output is often wrong, P31.
units.anchor: AI tools, such as ChatGPT, frequently fabricate information and invent references

units.why: 'provide clear instructions about which tools and resources can be used' asks faculty to spell out allowed AI, P09 (state expectations).
units.anchor: provide clear instructions about which tools and resources can be used

units.why: 'how to cite and acknowledge them' asks faculty to tell students how to cite AI tools, P24 (disclose/cite).
units.anchor: how to cite and acknowledge them
units.fit_note: Directed at instructors to explain how to cite; it does not itself require students to cite.

units.why: 'discuss them in class and point out the policies on the syllabus' asks faculty to talk through AI rules with students, P66.
units.anchor: discuss them in class and point out the policies on the syllabus

units.why: 'remind students regularly of Rutgers Academic Integrity policy' is repeated communication of the integrity rules; nearest is P66 (go beyond listing the rule).
units.anchor: remind students regularly of Rutgers Academic Integrity policy
units.fit_note: Reminders of the integrity policy rather than reasons behind AI rules.

units.why: 'require students to show stages of their work, e.g. outlines, rough drafts' asks for process artifacts to discourage AI use; P26 (keep and submit drafts).
units.anchor: require students to show stages of their work, e.g. outlines, rough drafts, selected references
units.fit_note: Process evidence is requested to deter AI, not to document disclosed AI use.

units.why: Major assignments 'submitted in a sequence of steps, which is known as scaffolding' restructure assignments around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Major assignments can be designed to be submitted in a sequence of steps

units.why: Suggests rubrics scoring 'critical thinking, problem-solving and application of knowledge' over summary; grading redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Use rubrics that score critical thinking, problem-solving and application of knowledge over summary and review.

units.why: Suggests students 'add personal comments such as reflections on the value of the assignment'; a redesign of assignments around AI, P35 rather than P26 because it is a deterrent device, not AI-use disclosure.
units.anchor: students can be required to add personal comments such as reflections on the value of

units.why: Suggests asking students to 'cite class readings or discussion' or use recent scholarship 'not available in AI databases'; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: ask that students cite class readings or discussion, or require that they use recent scholarship

units.why: Suggests sharing findings 'in a multimedia presentation, blog or podcast, webpage or e-portfolio' instead of text; format change in assignments, P35.
units.anchor: might be shared in a multimedia presentation, blog or podcast, webpage or e-portfolio

units.why: Lists a use: 'use as personalized tutor for improving learning'; AI as tutor, P12.
units.anchor: use as personalized tutor for improving learning

units.why: Lists a use: 'create questions for content knowledge self-assessments'; study aid and self-check, P14.
units.anchor: create questions for content knowledge self-assessments

units.why: Lists a use: 'generate opposing arguments for discussions'; exploring alternative viewpoints, P15.
units.anchor: generate opposing arguments for discussions

units.why: Lists a use: 'use to organize ideas in a first draft'; AI for writing support, P18.
units.anchor: use to organize ideas in a first draft

notes: Coder B. Only the two included universitywide documents were coded. Not coded: OTEAR navigation, event descriptions, reading and tool lists (links to third-party items, not Rutgers policy). The OTEAR page is marked archived and no longer maintained. The three sample syllabus statements appear twice on the page; the repeat in the FAQ was not coded again. Sample statements are coded as options offered to instructors, not as mandated rules.
